newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN health agency calls for more Madcow studies.
newsitem.headline: UN health agency calls for more Madcow studies.

text.p: The World Health Organisation (WHO) called on Tuesday for more scientific studies so as to validate the latest evidence that people can get a new human form of mad cow disease from beef.
The United Nations health agency, in a statement, also confirmed that it would host the next meeting of international experts on Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) early in 1997.
British scientists last week provided more evidence that BSE was linked to a new variant of the human brain-wasting disorder, Creutzfeld-Jakob Disease, which hits people under the age of 40.
WHO, referring to new scientific data on the possible transmission of BSE to humans published recently in Nature magazine, said:

"The molecular marker identified by these experiments should be useful for epidemiological studies of CJD and animal transmissible spongiform encephalopathies and for the differential diagnosis of new variant CJD in suspect cases.
"Further collaborative studies would be useful to validate the method described in the article, however," it added.

"To fully understand the relationship between BSE and human disease, additional retrospective and prospective case-control studies on the new variant form of CJD are required, as well as transmission studies in laboratory animals models, especially transgenic mice using certain tissues and derived products from BSE-infected cattle."
No WHO experts were available for further comment on the two-page statement, which was issued late in the day.

Last April and May, the Geneva-based WHO hosted two sessions bringing together neurologists, epidemiologists and laboratory specialists from Europe and North America to examine whether control policies were adequate to minimise the risk of human exposure to mad cow disease.
The experts agreed that worldwide surveillance, coordinated by the WHO, should be carried out on all transmissible BSEs, whether in humans or animals.
